summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: In a suit over a child's death, the Court held that a public children services agency and its employees owe no R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) duty to cross-report an incoming referral to law enforcement, that R.C. 2919.22 does not expressly impose liability on them, and that employee immunity is lost only for recklessness, which requires a perverse disregard of a known risk rather than mere negligence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Ohio Supreme Court decision on agency and caseworker immunity when a child dies under agency supervision.
key_cases.quote: a public children services agency and its employees, upon receipt of a case referral, do not have a duty under R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) to cross-report the case to a law-enforcement agency

key_cases.case_name: Yates v. Mansfield Bd. of Edn.
key_cases.holding: A board of education may be held liable under former R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) when its failure to report a teacher's sexual abuse of one student in violation of R.C. 2151.421 proximately results in the same teacher's sexual abuse of a different student.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Ohio case allowing recovery where a suppressed report allowed a known abuser continued access to children.
key_cases.quote: R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) requires designated persons to "immediately report" their "knowledge or suspicion" that a child "has suffered or faces a threat of suffering" any injury indicative of abuse or neglect

key_cases.holding: Because R.C. 2151.421 commands designated professionals to report and R.C. 2151.99 criminally penalizes the failure to do so, the statute 'expressly imposes liability' within R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) and 2744.03(A)(6)(c), stripping a political subdivision and its employees of statutory immunity for a failure to report.
key_cases.relevance: When a child is seriously harmed after a professional failed to report, Campbell supplies the immunity exception that permits a damages claim against the subdivision.
key_cases.quote: we hold that within the meaning of R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) and 2744.03(A)(6)(c), R.C. 2151.421 expressly imposes liability for failure to perform the duty to report known or suspected child abuse

key_cases.case_name: Gersper v. Ashtabula County Children Services Board
key_cases.holding: Former R.C. 2151.421(G) immunized a children services board and its caseworker from a negligent-investigation suit because, although as recipients of the report they were not 'participating in the making of reports,' they did participate in the judicial proceeding that resulted from the report; the Court distinguished Brodie, where the agency received reports of abuse and failed to act at all.
key_cases.relevance: Read with Brodie, Gersper marks the boundary between immunized action on a report and the unprotected failure to act that precedes a child's serious injury.
key_cases.quote: former R.C. 2151.421(G) confers immunity upon those who, as a result of a report of a known or suspected incident of child abuse and/or neglect, participate in a judicial proceeding

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, Seventh Appellate District, Belmont County
key_cases.holding: Affirming immunity for a school district and its administrators in a suit arising from a teacher's abuse of students, the court held that the R.C. 2151.421 reporting duty and the R.C. 2151.421(N) damages remedy run against the individual mandated reporters rather than against the political subdivision, and that liability attaches only where the individual had reason to suspect the abuse and failed to report.
key_cases.relevance: It shows how Ohio courts now allocate responsibility after a child is abused by a school employee, and it is a necessary check on reading Campbell as imposing liability on the district itself under the current statute.
key_cases.quote: Civil liability pursuant to R.C. 2151.421 only attaches when the duty to report abuse is violated.
